title: Environmental excellence in Saudi Arabia: Governance, achievements, and strategic opportunities — a systematic review (PRISMA 2020)
summary: Under Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia has rebuilt its environmental governance around the 2020/21 Environment Law, the National Center for Environmental Compliance, the Saudi Green Initiative (SGI), and ISO 14001/EIA alignment. This review sets out that framework, draws together outcomes across biodiversity, air, water, waste, and climate/energy, and flags priority gaps for Vision 2030 and comparable jurisdictions. The search, conducted to PRISMA 2020 standards, covered Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar, supplemented by reference-list and grey-literature screening against a pre-specified PECO frame. All records were screened by the author; a second screener dual-screened a 20% sample. Quality was appraised with JBI checklists, and certainty was rated using a GRADE-informed approach. Of 3,512 records screened after de-duplication, 78 sources met inclusion criteria, spanning six domains: governance and compliance institutions; biodiversity (protected-area coverage grew from ~4% to 18.1% of land); air quality (~240 stations; declining PM2.5, NOx, SO2); water (>200 plants; 100% urban-reuse target); waste (2021 Waste Management Law; 85-90% diversion by 2035-2040); and clean energy/climate (50% renewable electricity by 2030; net-zero by 2060; expanding CCUS/hydrogen). Certainty was moderate for governance, low to moderate for environmental quality (largely government reports), and low for projections. Vision 2030 has substantially expanded the Kingdom's environmental institutions, laws, and infrastructure, with real progress in protected areas, monitoring, wastewater reuse, and renewables. Still, the evidence base leans heavily on descriptive policy sources, and independent long-term evaluation remains thin. Priorities ahead: independent monitoring and verification, disaggregated outcome data, and replication in comparable arid, hydrocarbon-exporting jurisdictions.

title: Governing critical AI capabilities through sovereign orchestration without full stack ownership
summary: Abstract AI increasingly depends on globally distributed infrastructures, including advanced semiconductors, cloud platforms, data centres, foundation models, software frameworks and specialised labour. This dependence has intensified policy interest in AI sovereignty, which is often associated with domestic ownership of technological assets and the development of a nationally controlled AI stack. This article argues that ownership is neither a sufficient nor universally necessary condition of sovereign control. Instead, AI sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of public authorities to govern the dependencies through which critical AI capabilities are produced, accessed and sustained. The article develops the concept of functional AI sovereignty and identifies six interdependent dimensions of effective sovereign control: visibility, authority, allocation, substitutability, continuity and accountability. It then introduces sovereign orchestration as an institutional model through which governments can coordinate heterogeneous public and private AI resources using regulation, strategic procurement, interoperability, multi-provider routing, capacity clearing and selective public ownership. This model seeks to preserve access to private investment, international supply chains and distributed expertise while preventing individual providers from acquiring an irreversible veto over critical public functions. The article also specifies the limits of functional sovereignty. Orchestration requires sufficient public-sector expertise, access to operational information and credible technological alternatives. Direct ownership remains necessary where interruption costs are high, substitution is infeasible and external legal or geopolitical exposure is substantial. Effective AI sovereignty therefore lies not in eliminating technological interdependence, but in ensuring that critical dependencies remain visible, reversible, resilient and publicly accountable.

title: Mediating Role of Digital Culture in the Relationship between Digital Leadership and Sustainable Organizational Performance
summary: The fast-growing pace of digital transformation encourages organizations to strengthen their leadership and cultural competencies that foster economic, social and environmental values. Grounded in resource-based view theory, the current study examines how digital culture mediates the relationship between digital leadership and sustainable organizational performance in the selected financial institutions in the Nuwara-Eliya district of Sri Lanka. A quantitative, cross sectional study design was employed to achieve the study objectives by collecting primary data from 228 employees from the leading financial institutions, utilizing a proportionate simple random sampling technique. Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS 26.0) was applied to test hypothesized relationships among the constructs. Findings revealed a strong and positive relationship among digital leadership, digital culture and sustainable organizational performance. Further, mediation analysis demonstrated that digital culture partially mediates this relationship. The study highlights the importance of cultivating digital leadership capabilities and nurturing a supportive digital culture to achieve long-term sustainability. The findings provide empirical evidence for existing literature and valuable insights for managers and policymakers seeking to improve organizational sustainability in the era of digital transformation.

title: Drivers of Enterprise Resilience Under Compound Shocks: A PLS-SEM Analysis of Vietnamese Firms and Cooperatives
summary: Between 2020 and 2022, enterprises in emerging economies faced a succession of overlapping shocks—the COVID-19 pandemic, the supply-chain and energy consequences of the Russia–Ukraine conflict, and a sharp tightening of credit conditions—that tested their capacity to absorb losses, keep operating and adapt. Yet we still know little about which capabilities are associated with resilience, because most studies look at large firms in developed economies and test one capability at a time. This study asks which capabilities are most strongly associated with the resilience of small and medium-sized enterprises and cooperatives facing compound shocks, and through which pathways these associations run. Drawing on the dynamic-capabilities view and the resource-based view, an integrative model of six capabilities—anticipatory preparedness, leadership dynamism, institutional and government support, organizational social capital, human-resource resilience and digital transformation—is tested on survey data from 345 Vietnamese enterprises and cooperatives using PLS-SEM, with mediation analysis, common-method diagnostics and robustness checks. The findings suggest that human-resource resilience is the strongest correlate of perceived resilience, whereas institutional and government support is the only capability also associated with faster outcome-based recovery. Managers should treat workforce development and digital adoption as core resilience investments rather than discretionary costs, and state support programs should pair the financial and administrative assistance firms demand with the skilling and digitalization support that is most strongly associated with resilience in these data.

title: STRATEGI KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT UNTUK PENGEMBANGAN SUMBERDAYA MANUSIA DALAM TRANSFORMASI DIGITAL BANK TABUNGAN NEGARA
summary: Digital transformation has become a strategic priority in the banking industry, requiring organizations to strengthen not only technological capabilities but also human resource competencies. Knowledge Management (KM) plays a crucial role in supporting human resource development by facilitating knowledge creation, acquisition, storage, sharing, and application. This study aims to analyze the implementation of Knowledge Management as a human resource development strategy to support digital transformation at PT Bank Tabungan Negara (Persero) Tbk. A qualitative approach with a case study design was employed. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, observations, and document analysis involving managers and employees directly engaged in Knowledge Management and human resource development initiatives. Data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings indicate that Knowledge Management has evolved beyond information management into a strategic organizational capability that enhances digital competencies, organizational learning, innovation, and employee adaptability. The implementation of Learning Management Systems, knowledge sharing, coaching, mentoring, and communities of practice significantly strengthens workforce readiness for digital transformation. Leadership commitment, learning culture, and digital infrastructure were identified as key enabling factors, while differences in digital competencies, resistance to change, and limited knowledge-sharing practices remain major challenges. The study concludes that Knowledge Management is a strategic mechanism for developing human capital and ensuring sustainable digital transformation in the banking sector.Keywords: Digital transformation, Human resource development, Knowledge management, Learning organization, Organizational learning

title: Implementation of an Integrated Agricultural and Fisheries System in Padeg Village, Gresik Regency
summary: Agriculture in Indonesia is currently facing significant pressure due to climate change. Agricultural systems that are highly dependent on climatic conditions and rely solely on rainwater are particularly vulnerable to these impacts. Extreme weather conditions, such as prolonged dry seasons, can lead to drought, reducing agricultural productivity and even causing farmers to lose their sources of income. This study discusses the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) program of PT Pertamina Patra Niaga – Bitumen Plant Gresik, particularly the implementation of agricultural and fisheries integration in Padeg Village, Gresik Regency, where approximately 90% of the population are farmers. A unique characteristic of agriculture in this village is the absence of natural water sources. Nevertheless, farmers demonstrate strong commitment to agricultural innovation by integrating crop cultivation with fish farming, adopting agricultural technologies, and developing independent fish hatchery through biofloc technology. This integration serves as an effort to improve agricultural productivity and efficiency while promoting the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of the community.

title: Where, but not who: Why India's largest companies cannot say where their CSR goes, and how a five-rung test would show whom it reaches
summary: Since 2014, India has required its largest companies to spend 2 percent of their profits on corporate social responsibility, and the amount is now substantial: the National CSR Portal records Rs 40,131 crore (US$4.80 billion) spent in 2024-25. Because the law names social ends, including ending hunger and poverty and reducing the inequalities faced by socially and economically backward groups, we can judge its money only by who received it and what changed for them. The filings that account for it answer a different question: where the money went, and for most of the money, they do not even answer that. This working paper tests the record against a five-rung ladder: where the money landed, who it passed through, who received it, what position they held relative to the rule that selected them, and whether it made a difference in their lives. For the 357 companies that spent at least Rs 10 crore between 2014 and 2020, Rs 55,857 crore (US$8.25 billion) in all, only 11.8 percent of the money names a district, and 302 of the 357 companies record a district for less than half of what they spent. Of the 55 companies that do record where, 26 fail a test of reach to the tail end, and 10 of those reach aspirational districts but not the tribal-majority districts within them. No filing reaches the four higher rungs. The paper argues that the gap is not a shortage of money or goodwill but a design choice in what the law asks companies to record, and it sets out how the Tail-End Assessment would close it.

title: Internal Control Systems and Financial Reporting Quality: The Moderating Role of Firm Leverage in Non-Financial Firms Listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange
summary: This study examined whether firm leverage moderates the association between internal control systems and financial reporting quality among non-financial firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). Financial reporting quality is essential to investor confidence and effective capital-market oversight, yet internal control systems may not deliver uniform outcomes across firms facing different financial pressures. The study used a positivist philosophy, a deductive approach and an explanatory longitudinal panel design. Secondary data were drawn from annual reports, audited financial statements and corporate-governance disclosures for 26 firms selected from a population of 39 non-financial listed firms that met the stated continuous-listing and data-availability criteria, covering 2010–2025 (416 firm-year observations). Internal controls were operationalised through an Internal Control Disclosure Index (ICDI) based on the five COSO components; leverage was measured as total liabilities divided by total assets; and financial reporting quality was proxied by the inverse of discretionary accruals estimated using the modified Jones model. Fixed-effects panel regression with firm-clustered robust standard errors showed a positive association between the ICDI and reporting quality (β = 1.497, p < .001) and a positive direct association between leverage and reporting quality (β = 0.566, p < .001). The interaction term was negative and statistically significant (β = −1.767, p < .001), indicating that the positive association between disclosed internal controls and reporting quality weakened as leverage increased. The study recommends that regulators, boards and lenders should assess internal-control disclosures alongside leverage exposure. This study provides evidence on how internal controls affect financial reporting quality, accountability, and the reliability of financial information.

title: Family Ownership, External Audit, and Informal Payments: Evidence for Corporate Governance and Regulatory Compliance in the MENA Region
summary: This study investigates the association between family ownership and informal payments and examines how external audit certification conditions this relationship. Using a sample of 4161 firms from Morocco, Egypt, Tunisia, and Jordan drawn from the EBRD–EIB–World Bank Enterprise Surveys, the empirical analysis employs logit and probit regression models, supplemented by adjusted predicted probabilities and probability contrasts. The findings reveal a significant positive association between family-majority ownership and informal payments in the additive models, consistent with governance concerns arising from concentrated family control. Furthermore, while external audit certification is negatively associated with informal payments, the positive and significant interaction coefficient suggests that this association may be weaker within family-majority firms. However, the difference between the estimated audit contrasts is not statistically significant on the probability scale, providing partial support for this moderating relationship. These results suggest a possible ownership-related boundary condition on formal external monitoring. This pattern may be consistent with institutional decoupling, although the organizational mechanisms underlying the observed association remain to be established. The study concludes that the relationship between external auditing and informal payments should be considered alongside ownership structure, highlighting the importance of examining auditor independence, audit quality, and internal governance arrangements beyond the mere presence of external certification.

title: ALGORITHMIC PERSONALIZATION AND CONSUMER TRUST IN EMERGING DIGITAL MARKETS: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR MARKETING MANAGEMENT IN UZBEKISTAN
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central instrument of contemporary marketing, particularly in the form of algorithmic personalization of offers, messages and recommendations. While the literature in advanced economies documents both the commercial value of personalization and the consumer resistance it can provoke, emerging digital markets remain comparatively underexplored. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework that explains how the quality of AI-driven personalization translates into purchase intention and loyalty in an emerging-market setting, using Uzbekistan as the reference context. Drawing on research on AI in marketing, algorithm aversion, organizational trust and information privacy, the paper positions consumer trust in the AI system as the key mediating mechanism and identifies algorithmic transparency and perceived human oversight as its principal antecedents. Perceived privacy risk and decision involvement are proposed as boundary conditions, and linguistic and cultural fit is introduced as a context-specific component of personalization quality. Five testable propositions are formulated, a four-phase research design is outlined, and managerial implications are presented for firms operating in mobile-first, multilingual markets with fast-growing e-commerce and fintech sectors. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation.

title: How ESG dimensions shape corporate green innovation: Necessary-condition thresholds, causal asymmetry, and the resource curse
summary: Whether ESG dimensions shape green innovation through consistent mechanisms remains contested, in part because ESG rating divergence can alter empirical conclusions. Using three independent ESG data sources (Huazheng, CNRDS, Runling Global) and a multi-method design (fixed effects, NCA, fsQCA) covering Chinese listed firms (2015–2023), we document a construct-asymmetry thesis : ESG dimensions do not have uniform roles across rating sources. In the Huazheng sample, Governance (G) and Environmental (E) dimensions are necessary conditions for substantive green innovation (d > 0.28); in two independent ratings, the necessity pattern shifts toward the Social (S) dimension, while G necessity disappears. This divergence is not an artifact of sample composition — it persists in a matched same-firm sample — but reflects systematic differences in how rating agencies operationalize governance and social responsibility. Despite this measurement sensitivity, failure configurations are more identifiable than success recipes — a pattern consistent with the panel and NCA evidence across sources — and the average facilitative effect of G on strategic innovation is directionally consistent. Our findings suggest that the ESG–green innovation relationship is more method- and construct-dependent than previously assumed, and that multi-source validation is indispensable for credible ESG–innovation research.

summary: Digital transformation changes the competencies organizations need, so competency matrices must be rethought as tools linking business needs with human resource (HR) development. This study synthesizes how the competency-strategy matrix is transformed in the digital era. A systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA 2020 was applied to journal articles from Google Scholar, Garuda, Neliti, and Scopus. The matrix evolves through administrative, strategy-linked, and digitally adaptive stages. Digital transformation shifts competency demands toward digital, data, and behavioral skills, while technologies such as enterprise systems and artificial intelligence bring efficiency but also the risk of dehumanization. The study proposes an integrative framework and a research agenda.

title: Embedding sustainability in higher education: a decade-long systematic review of global best practices, emerging trends and future pathways
summary: Purpose This study systematically examines how higher education institutions have embedded sustainability across teaching, research, governance, operations and community engagement between 2015 and 2025. It seeks to analyze the organizational mechanisms, tensions and governance dynamics that shape sustainability institutionalization and produce divergent trajectories across institutions. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 126 peer reviewed articles from Scopus indexed Q1 and A ranked journals were analyzed. A combined inductive and deductive coding strategy informed by organizational theory was applied across five domains: campus operations, curriculum development, research and innovation, governance and policy and community engagement. Thematic synthesis and bibliometric mapping were used to identify recurring patterns, cross domain dynamics and structural imbalances in the literature. Findings The findings indicate that sustainability embedding in higher education unfolds as a paradoxical organizational process rather than a linear progression of best practices. While formal governance mechanisms, ESG reporting and sustainability rankings increase institutional commitment and visibility, implementation remains uneven and frequently fragmented across domains. Recurring patterns include partial institutionalization, symbolic compliance, stakeholder driven adaptation and governance constraints. Emerging trends include digital transformation, intensified accountability pressures and context specific localization aligned with the SDGs. Persistent challenges relate to capacity gaps, decentralized authority and misalignment between formal strategy and everyday academic practice. Originality/value By reframing sustainability embedding as an organizational behavior phenomenon, this review advances organization theory by explaining how institutional pressures interact with loosely coupled academic structures to shape uneven transformation. The study offers a theory of informed synthesis that moves beyond descriptive aggregation toward a conceptual understanding of sustainability institutionalization in complex organizations.

title: The Contribution of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) to Public Management Reform: The Case of African Administrations
summary: This research examines the contribution of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR, or RSO in French contexts) to public management reform within African administrations. Addressing the structural circularity and conceptual limitations of traditional "catch-all" frameworks, we restructure the theoretical model into a sequential system of systemic relational mediation. Utilizing a multiple case study design encompassing ten public administrations across four African countries (Morocco, Senegal, Nigeria, and Sudan), primary data were collected through sixteen in-depth semi-structured interviews and supplemented by two focus groups. A thematic analysis demonstrates the pivotal role of Politico-Administrative Responsibility (PAR, or RPA). The streamlined model reveals that external environmental pressures from citizen-clients significantly heighten internal operational tensions between public managers and politicians. In response, this friction stimulates the co-construction and activation of a shared PAR framework. Acting as a central regulatory lever, PAR effectively reduces internal organizational conflict and, consequently, restores institutional trust while fostering the success of administrative modernization.

title: The Impact of Digital Skills on Common Prosperity for Rural and Pastoral Households in Underdeveloped Regions
summary: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence and digital tools, the digital economy has become an important driving force for socioeconomic development, and digital skills have become a crucial capability for achieving common prosperity. Based on 804 pieces of micro-survey data from agricultural and pastoral areas in Xizang, this study explores common prosperity from the objective material dimension and subjective spiritual dimension, starting with the economic effect and social effect of digital skills. It constructs a dual-path analysis framework of “digital skills–economic behavior–common prosperity” and “digital skills–social psychology–common prosperity” to theoretically analyze and empirically test the logical relationship and mechanism of action of digital skills on the common prosperity of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions. The research indicates that digital skills significantly promote the common prosperity of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions, with a greater impact on spiritual common prosperity than material common prosperity. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the promotion effect of digital skills on common prosperity is more pronounced in villages located in relatively economically developed agricultural areas, indicating the existence of certain digital poverty and a digital divide. The mechanism analysis shows that digital skills affect common prosperity through two paths: non-agricultural employment in economic behavior and fairness perception in social psychology. Therefore, it is necessary to improve digital infrastructure in agricultural and pastoral areas and enhance the digital skills of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions; improve the information release and transmission mechanism of digital platforms to promote non-agricultural employment; enhance digital social inclusiveness and digital cultural regulation to improve fairness perception; and leverage the empowering and converging effects of the digital economy, harness the economic effect and social effect of digital skills, and enhance both material and spiritual common prosperity to achieve comprehensive common prosperity.

title: Pentahelix Collaboration as a Strategy for CSR Program Sustainability: A Case Study of Women-Headed Household Cocoa Farmers Empowerment
summary: The long-term viability of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programs depends not only on corporate investment but also on effective multi-stakeholder collaboration. This report examines the implementation of the Pentahelix collaboration model as a strategy for strengthening the sustainability of the Women-Headed Household Cocoa Farmers Empowerment Program (INONG BALEE), implemented by PT Pertamina Hulu Energi North Sumatra Offshore (PHE NSO) in Blang Pante Village, North Aceh Regency. The program was developed from a biodiversity conservation initiative aimed at reducing human–wildlife conflict through community-based economic empowerment. This study employs a qualitative approach using a case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and company documentation. The findings indicate that the Pentahelix model engages five key stakeholder groups in various stages of the program cycle, including planning, implementation, facilitation, monitoring, and evaluation. Their collaborative engagement enables the integration of resources, knowledge, and institutional capacities to support program implementation. Based on these findings, this study proposes the Pentahelix Sustainability Collaboration Model (PSCM) as a conceptual framework for strengthening the long-term viability of CSR programs through shared roles, resource integration, institutional engagement, and continuous collaboration beyond corporate intervention.

title: Abu Ubaid's Thoughts on the Economy of the People: a Case Study of Community-Based Economic Management in the Digital World
summary: Abu Ubaid's thoughts on the ummah economy, which includes the principles of distributional justice, property protection, social solidarity, and the role of the state in regulating markets, are still relevant to apply in community-based economic management, especially in the digital world. As sharia-based digital platforms develop, it is important to understand how these principles can be adapted to create a more inclusive and fair economy. This research aims to analyze the relevance of Abu Ubaid's thoughts in the context of a digital community-based economy, as well as exploring its application in platforms such as digital cooperatives, sharia crowdfunding, and sharia marketplaces. This research uses a qualitative approach with case studies on several digital community platforms that implement sharia principles. Data was collected through document analysis, interviews with platform managers, and observations of platform operational practices. The research results show that the principles of wealth as trust, kifayah (sufficiency), and distribution of wealth through zakat, alms, and fa'i are very relevant to digital community-based economic practices. These platforms integrate sharia contracts such as mudharabah, musyarakah and murabahah, and provide transparency features such as periodic reports and financial dashboards. However, most platforms refer more to contemporary muamalah fiqh and modern sharia standards, with Abu Ubaid's thoughts rarely being explicitly referenced. This research suggests the integration of zakat, waqf and infaq principles into digital platform design, as well as the preparation of community economic guidelines based on classical scientific heritage. Collaboration between classical jurisprudence experts, sharia fintech practitioners, and technology developers will help translate Abu Ubaid's principles into applicable technical features.

title: Cloud-Based Infrastructure for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Workloads: A Scalable Framework for Saudi Enterprises
summary: In Saudi companies artificial intelligence and machine learning are moving from being mere experiments to becoming operational capabilities, which is leading to an infrastructure issue that goes well beyond the need for computing power. The processes involved in training, fine-tuning, inference, feature preparation, model monitoring, governance and retraining all have diverse requirements for accelerators, storage, networking, data locality, elasticity and reliability. This review draws on research carried out between 2020 and 2025 in order to look at how cloud architecture can support these types of workloads on an enterprise level while taking into account the Saudi situation regarding rapid digital transformation, the adoption of cloud services, data governance and the modernisation of various sectors. The review applies a structured evidence-synthesis approach focused on infrastructure architecture, workload orchestration, MLOps, cloud-edge distribution, security, reliability, cost control and organisational readiness. The evidence shows that scalable AI infrastructure should be viewed as a coordinated platform rather than as a set of separate services; effective designs incorporate elastic pools of CPU and GPU resources, container orchestration, tiered data services, automated model pipelines, observability, policy controls, workload-aware scheduling and selective edge execution. The Saudi Enterprise AI Cloud Framework proposed in this review combines these capabilities into six layers and includes a closed operational loop that links demand prediction, placement, execution, telemetry, policy evaluation and lifecycle learning. The review maintains that scalability must be assessed together with availability, cost predictability, data sovereignty, operational resilience and discipline in managing the model lifecycle. It ends with an implementation roadmap and a research agenda for businesses that wish to industrialise AI as part of their digital transformation aligned with Vision 2030.

title: Financial Shared Services at SAIC Motor: Market Response and Outcomes
summary: Under the background of digital transformation of enterprises, the financial sharing center has gradually transformed from accounting reimbursement center to data value creation center, and the construction of financial sharing architecture of large diversified groups has become a hot spot in practice. This paper takes SAIC as a research case to explore the market performance and implementation effect of the financial sharing model of automobile manufacturing diversification group. It is found that SAIC has achieved results in reducing operating costs, strengthening capital risk management and promoting the integration of industry and finance by adopting the differentiated path of building financial sharing centers in different sectors, but at the same time, there are practical pain points such as non-uniform standards, insufficient cross-departmental coordination, redundant approval process and difficult personnel transformation. This study enriches the case study of financial sharing of automobile diversification groups and provides practical reference for similar large-scale automobile enterprises to optimize the construction of financial sharing and release the value of digital financial management.

title: Emerging Trends in AI, Data Science and Cloud-Based Technologies
summary: The fusion of artificial intelligence (AI), data science, and cloud computing technologies is transforming the nature of the digital economy from disconnected technological silos to interdependent ecosystems that complement each other. This paper explores current trends within these interrelated fields such as world models, agentic AI systems, cloud-native AI integration, and industrialization of data science. Mixed methods of research including the systematic literature review combined with the quantitative analysis of industry data is suggested. Convergence patterns analysis shows that cloud platforms transform from mere infrastructure into smart services ecosystems, and data science changes from disconnected modeling into engineering practice. Comparative analysis shows that companies embracing integrated approach to cloud-AI-data management enjoy considerably lower training costs and reduced deployment timeframes. The conclusion is made about the challenges related to governance, skill development, and infrastructure sustainability that need addressing.

title: Turning data into green action: how the environmental value of digitalization emerges in maritime supply chains
summary: As digital transformation accelerates and environmental regulations become more stringent, increasing attention has been paid to how maritime firms translate digital resources into environmental value. Drawing on organizational information processing theory and the natural resource-based view, this study develops a multistage model to examine the relationship between supply chain digitalization and environmental performance. The model focuses on an information-processing pathway reflected in supply chain visibility and a supplier-coordination pathway reflected in green supply chain collaboration, highlighting the connecting role of firms’ internal green responses. Using 253 valid questionnaire responses from Chinese maritime logistics firms, the model was tested through covariance-based structural equation modeling. The results show that supply chain digitalization is positively and significantly associated with both supply chain visibility and green supply chain collaboration, although the two capabilities exhibit distinct downstream patterns of association. Supply chain visibility is positively and significantly associated with both internal environmental management and green operational practices, whereas green supply chain collaboration is positively and significantly associated only with green operational practices; its association with internal environmental management is not statistically significant. Both internal green responses are positively and significantly associated with improvements in perceived environmental performance. These findings reveal differences in how information processing and supplier coordination connect with firms’ internal green responses, deepen the understanding of how digital resources are translated into environmental value in the maritime context, and offer practical implications for aligning digitalization initiatives with green management.

title: Exploring How Audit Quality Bridges the Link between Board Audit Committee Financial Expertise and Financial Reporting Quality: Empirical Evidence from Kenyan Commercial Banks
summary: Financial reporting quality (FRQ) within the banking industry is of particular interest due to the importance of transparency, market confidence and financial stability. Banks are particularly prone to FRQ issues due to the high level of estimation within the accounting process such as loan loss provisions (LLP). In addition, low FRQ may mask risk and pose a threat to financial stability. This study sought to establish the mediating effect of audit quality on the relationship between board audit committee financial expertise and financial reporting quality (FRQ) among banks in Kenya. Anchored on Agency Theory, Stakeholder Theory and Resource Dependence Theory, the study adopted a positivist philosophy and an explanatory longitudinal panel research design. Secondary data were obtained from audited financial statements, annual reports, external audit reports and Central Bank of Kenya publications covering 2015–2024, and all analyses were based on this full balanced panel of 330 observations. Financial reporting quality was measured using absolute discretionary loan-loss provisions derived from a bank-specific loan-loss-provision model, with lower values indicating less reporting discretion and higher financial reporting quality. Audit quality was proxied by external audit fees. Mediation was tested using the Sobel test. The mediation results demonstrated that audit quality mediate the relationship between financial expertise (indirect β = 0.008, p < 0.05), meeting frequency (indirect β = 0.007, p < 0.05), independence (indirect β = 0.005, p < 0.05) and size (indirect β = 0.005, p < .05) and financial reporting quality. The study recommends that banks and regulators should strengthen substantive board audit committee financial expertise and engagement between Board Audit Committees and external auditors. The findings have the potential to provide policymakers and regulators with information highlighting the significance of strong audit board committee in the process of enhancing financial reporting quality. title: Integrating Lean Six Sigma and Industry 4.0: drivers for enhancing competitiveness in large industrial companies
summary: Purpose This study aims to propose a set of drivers for integrating Lean Six Sigma (LSS) and Industry 4.0 (I4) in large industrial companies to enhance synergies and mitigate dissonances between these approaches, thereby improving operational efficiency and profitability and increasing organizational competitiveness. Design/methodology/approach A literature review established the theoretical framework and identified LSS–I4 synergies and dissonances. The findings were complemented by multiple case studies in four large companies, capturing practical barriers and lessons learned. The drivers were subsequently developed through the triangulation of literature, empirical evidence and expert validation. Findings The empirical evidence suggests that synergies between LSS and I4 can strengthen organizational learning, innovation capability, operational excellence and continuous improvement. The five proposed drivers (Foundation, Intelligent Resources, Smart and Flexible Processes, Powerful Projects and Operational Controls) offer pathways to reinforce synergies and mitigate dissonances. Research limitations/implications This study is limited to large industrial companies. Scientifically, this study advances understanding of how digital transformation reshapes continuous improvement paradigms. In practice, this study supports managers in developing agile, data-driven and sustainable operations, thereby improving quality and competitiveness. Originality/value This research provides new empirical evidence on how operational excellence and digital transformation can be strategically aligned to build more adaptive organizations.

title: INVESTOR BEHAVIOUR IN THE DIGITAL FINANCIAL ECOSYSTEM: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW
summary: Structured Abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study is to undertake the systematic review of academic paper on digital and financial technology to describe the impact of various digital and financial technologies on the behaviour of retail investor under several cognitive and influence their investment decision-making. The study includes internet, social media and social trading platform as a advanced communication channel and social trading application and a financial technology facilitating in execution of trading decision. Study design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review has been conducted of 94 academic work which includes published journals, conference proceedings, working papers and published books with the systematic search of academic works from several electronic databases to identify relevant studies even though there was research work released between 2000 and 2023. The publication of notable works began in 2014. The search terms included "technological advancements," "internet," "social media," "social trading applications," "trading applications”, "retail investors," "investor behaviour," and "investment decision-making and fintech. Findings: The paper suggest that the digital and financial technological variable collectively impact investor in not only in providing with financial information but also in decision making and trade execution. The increased accessibility to information and trading avenues has led to challenges, such as information overload and the potential for overconfidence in decision-making which results in impulsive and frequent trading affecting their return. Moreover, digital communication technology such as social media, one of the essential sources of information and opinion, also is to be credited with impacting investor sentiment and behaviour leading to herd behaviour and suboptimal return. Research limitations/implications: This paper reports that investors’ behaviour post digital and financial technology adoption have high potential for further study by various stakeholders in the field of behavioural finance from academia, practitioners to regulators. Practical implications: The paper summarizes the lessons which is of importance for the retail investor, implies that retail investor should be careful in relying too much on the digital technology in terms of fetching financial information and trade execution especially when they are not financial experts. Social implications: Under this study, investors can recognize various cognitive biases that can influence their trading behavior and impact their returns. Originality/value: The paper add value in the understanding of digital and financial technological evolution and its impact, post-adoption, on the retail investors’ behaviour

title: Managing DX Risk of IT Project Failures by the Management
summary: Massive loss incidents have been repeatedly observed at companies, that tried DX (digital transformation of their business) and ordered vendors to develop necessary IT systems; the IT system development projects failed. IT disputes started between the companies and the vendors to compensate for individual loss, and claims by the companies for damages were finally dismissed by the courts. This paper first clarifies the facts of both the phenomena and the causes of IT project failures by analyzing public court records. Based on the analysis, we next derive and clarify business management methods for the prevention of recurrence of the losses and the IT disputes, as lessons learned. We also show actual amounts of the massive losses avoided by practicing business management methods, as rationale of this study. We also discuss how more companies should introduce business management methods globally.

title: Strategic financing and sustainability decisions in dual-channel supply chains under demand uncertainty: a distribution-free game-theoretic perspective
summary: Purpose This study investigates how financing structure and sustainability investment jointly influence pricing, service, and green decision-making in a dual-channel supply chain under demand uncertainty. It particularly examines how bank financing and trade credit shape firms' ability to improve environmental performance, strengthen channel competitiveness, and enhance customer value. Design/methodology/approach A Stackelberg game-theoretic model is developed involving a manufacturer and a retailer who operate through both online and offline channels. The manufacturer invests in green innovation financed through bank borrowing, while the retailer chooses between bank financing with a wholesale price discount or trade credit with deferred payment. Demand is uncertain and influenced by green investment and retail service. A distribution-free approach is employed to derive robust equilibrium strategies without assuming a specific demand distribution. Findings Results show that financing choices critically shape sustainability-oriented decisions and channel coordination. Trade credit encourages higher green investment and retail service when financing costs are high, whereas bank financing is more effective under lower borrowing rates and stronger discount incentives. Demand uncertainty substantially affects inventory and profitability, particularly under high-variance settings. The distribution-free framework enhances decision robustness under uncertain market environments. Originality/value This study develops an integrated dual-channel supply chain framework combining green innovation, retail service, dual financing, and distribution-free demand modeling within a single analytical structure. It contributes to marketing intelligence by illustrating how financial structures and uncertainty jointly drive sustainable strategy formation and channel coordination. The findings provide actionable insights for managers seeking to align green innovation, retail service, and financing decisions to build competitive and sustainable supply chains.

title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Whistleblowing Systems, and Professional Skepticism in Higher-Education Fraud Detection
summary: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Conclusion: These results suggest that artificial intelligence supports fraud detection not by replacing auditors' professional judgment but by strengthening organizational preparedness to integrate intelligent technologies into governance frameworks. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

title: Predicting First Observed Appearance in a Corporate Governance Rating List and Subsequent Upgrades with Interpretable Machine Learning
summary: Corporate governance certification provides a public assessment of organizational practices. Previous research has primarily examined the relationship between certification and firm outcomes, while the timing of certification adoption represents a distinct prediction problem. This study examines whether the first observed appearance on a governance rating list and subsequent rating upgrades can be predicted using statutory accounting disclosures. Rating history is also incorporated into the upgrade model. The institutional setting is the Borsa Istanbul Corporate Governance Index, where licensed agencies evaluate four governance sections and eligibility is determined by published thresholds. The dataset combines rating records for 49 non-financial firms from 2013 to 2024 with financial statements from 438 listed non-financial firms. Two interpretable modeling modules employ an out-of-time design, with predictor variables measured before the corresponding outcomes. The entry module compares L2-regularized logistic regression, Firth-penalized logistic regression, and gradient-boosted trees within a discrete-time hazard specification. The trajectory module estimates next-year rating upgrade scores for rated firms using accounting information and rating history. Both linear entry models achieve areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve above 0.50, while the regularized logistic model shows a small positive difference in average precision relative to the training-prevalence benchmark. A single deflated firm-size measure provides discriminatory performance comparable to that of the multivariate entry models. The combined upgrade models achieve ROC areas close to 0.60, while models incorporating rating history achieve higher ROC areas than accounting-only models. Feature attributions also differ between the two tasks, with firm size playing a prominent role in entry predictions and rating history contributing more strongly to upgrade predictions. These findings identify the information sets associated with observed rating adoption and progression. The proposed framework provides rankings of candidate firms and feature-level explanations to support governance monitoring and outreach planning.

title: АДАПТИВНЕ СТРАТЕГІЧНЕ УПРАВЛІННЯ ПІДПРИЄМСТВАМИ НА ЗАСАДАХ РЕЗИЛЬЄНТНОСТІ
summary: The article investigates the theoretical and methodological foundations of adaptive strategic management of enterprises based on the concept of organizational resilience under conditions of high uncertainty, martial law, digital transformation, disruption of logistics chains, increasing cyber risks, and growing global turbulence. It is substantiated that the contemporary business environment is characterized by nonlinear development, multidimensional threats, and rapid changes in external factors, which necessitates a transition from traditional strategic management models to an adaptive management paradigm focused on ensuring long-term sustainability, flexibility, rapid recovery, and strategic transformation of enterprises. The purpose of the study is to develop the theoretical and methodological foundations of adaptive strategic management based on resilience principles, substantiate the conceptual framework for the formation of strategic resilience, and develop a comprehensive management model integrating dynamic capabilities, strategic flexibility, digital transformation, scenario planning, risk management, and organizational learning into a unified system for ensuring sustainable enterprise development. The methodological framework of the study is based on general scientific and specialized research methods, including the systemic, structural-functional, logical-analytical, comparative, process-oriented, scenario-based, and integrated approaches. The method of critical literature analysis was applied to synthesize contemporary concepts of organizational resilience, while conceptual modeling, structural decomposition of management processes, and theoretical synthesis of strategic management and organizational resilience approaches were used to develop the proposed management model. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the development of a conceptual model of adaptive strategic management based on resilience principles, which, unlike existing approaches, is founded on the cyclical interaction between strategic monitoring systems, enterprise dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring), adaptive strategic processes, resilience-oriented managerial decisions, and organizational learning mechanisms. A structural and functional model of adaptive strategic management is proposed, ensuring a continuous process of strategic adaptation, resource reconfiguration, competence renewal, and business model transformation in response to changes in the external environment. Furthermore, a system for assessing strategic resilience is developed, encompassing financial, operational, organizational, human resource, digital, and innovation dimensions, as well as an integrated strategic resilience index designed to monitor the strategic sustainability of enterprises. The main findings demonstrate that adaptive strategic management should be interpreted as a continuous process of strategic reconfiguration of resources, competencies, and business processes in response to environmental changes. The relationship between enterprise dynamic capabilities and the formation of strategic resilience is substantiated, the key principles of adaptive strategic management are identified, and a mechanism for implementing a resilience-oriented strategy is developed. The study confirms that digital transformation, scenario planning, risk management, organizational learning, and the development of partnership ecosystems are the principal drivers of strategic adaptability and long-term enterprise resilience. The practical significance of the obtained results lies in the possibility of applying the proposed model by Ukrainian enterprises to ensure business continuity, strengthen resilience to crisis impacts, accelerate post-crisis recovery, and create sustainable competitive advantages under martial law and in the context of post-war economic transformation.

summary: The purpose of the research -This article examines human capital assessment through the integration of heterogeneous data and artificial intelligence in the context of the digital economy.The study aims to identify the interrelationships among artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and human capital, and to empirically evaluate how these factors influence productivity. Research methodology -The research applies analysis, comparison, systematization, grouping, and generalization methods.Its empirical part is based on panel data covering the period 2010-2024 and obtained from open international statistical databases.The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, unit root tests, cointegration analysis, multivariate regression modeling, and Granger causality testing.This methodological approach allows a comprehensive assessment of the interaction between artificial intelligence, digital transformation, human capital, and productivity.Results of the research -The findings show that artificial intelligence has a significant positive impact on productivity, while human capital strongly reinforces this effect.Digital transformation also contributes positively through better data processing and resource allocation.The results confirm long-run relationships among the variables and identify artificial intelligence and human capital as major drivers of productivity growth.Originality and scientific novelty of the research -The study offers an integrated and multidimensional framework for evaluating human capital in the digital economy.

summary: The article develops conceptual foundations for forming a tactical planning mechanism for corporate social responsibility (CSR) under the transformation of the external environment. The research problem arises from the gap between long-term sustainability strategies and the daily implementation of social, environmental and ethical commitments. Rapid regulatory changes, economic volatility, technological renewal, labour-market shifts, climate risks, security threats and growing stakeholder expectations require enterprises to revise CSR priorities more frequently and to connect them with budgets, responsibilities and measurable outcomes. The purpose of the study is to design a management mechanism that translates strategic CSR goals into coordinated actions for a three-to-twelve-month planning horizon. Systems, process, stakeholder and portfolio approaches are used. The proposed mechanism is organised as a recurring cycle that includes monitoring of the external environment, updating the stakeholder map, identifying material issues, setting tactical priorities, forming a balanced portfolio of CSR initiatives, allocating resources and responsibility, implementation, communication, control and corrective managerial learning. Tactical initiatives are divided into four groups: mandatory compliance measures, risk-reduction measures, stakeholder-value projects and development-oriented initiatives. This classification helps avoid the fragmentation of CSR into unrelated charitable activities and supports the prioritisation of actions according to urgency, stakeholder significance, expected impact and resource feasibility. The article also proposes an indicator system covering implementation discipline, stakeholder response, employee outcomes, environmental effects, reputational results and the contribution of CSR measures to organisational resilience. The scientific novelty lies in interpreting tactical CSR planning as a rolling portfolio-management process rather than as a static annual list of social activities. The mechanism provides a practical link between sustainability strategy, external signals and operational decision-making. It may be used by enterprises when preparing annual and quarterly CSR plans, adapting programmes during crises, developing sustainability reporting and coordinating the actions of management, HR, environmental, compliance, communications and operational units.

title: ESG performance and financing constraints in aquaculture and fishery listed companies: Evidence from China
summary: This paper uses Chinese A-share fishery-listed companies from 2009 to 2025 as the research sample, comprising 14 companies and 197 annual panel observations. Using a two-way fixed-effects model, it empirically tests the impact, transmission path, and heterogeneity of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance on the financing constraints of fishery companies. The ESG indicators are measured using a comprehensive rating of 0 to 100 points on the Huazheng Index, with higher scores indicating better overall levels of environmental compliance, social responsibility fulfillment, and internal governance of the company. Financing constraints are calculated using the KZ index, with a higher index value indicating greater financing constraints for the company. The study found that the regression coefficient of the comprehensive ESG score of companies is -0.069, which is significantly negative at the 5% statistical level, indicating that good ESG performance can significantly alleviate the financing constraints of fishery companies. Mechanism testing shows that subsidy acquisition and supply chain relationship governance are the two core transmission channels through which ESG mitigates effects. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the environmental dimension is the core driver of ESG in improving the financing environment for companies, and that the financing slow-release effect of ESG is more pronounced in aquaculture and fishery companies with low export dependence. This study is based on the local characteristics of China’s fisheries industry policies and industrial chain, and examines the economic effects of ESG in the agricultural sector. It can provide local empirical evidence to optimize green finance policies in the fisheries industry and to lay out ESG practices for listed aquatic companies.

title: State-corporate crime in cryptocurrency markets: governance failure and insider abuse in Terra-Luna and FTX
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how governance design and regulatory fragmentation combined to enable the collapses of Terra-Luna and FTX and asks when state inaction in cryptocurrency markets can properly be analysed as state-facilitated corporate crime rather than ordinary regulatory lag. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative comparative case study of the two platforms, based on a documented inventory of criminal, civil, regulatory and bankruptcy records from 2022 to 2025, coded across three dimensions: governance architecture, insider abuse and state response. Findings Both platforms concentrated discretionary control in their founders and operated without independent oversight, reliable financial reporting or capital segregation, yet they failed through mechanisms specific to their designs: custody misuse in a centralised exchange at FTX and stability and reserve misrepresentation in an algorithmic stablecoin system at Terra-Luna. Applying four proposed criteria that distinguish regulatory lag from state facilitation, the state’s role in the FTX case approaches facilitation, while Terra-Luna sits closer to lag. Victims in both cases faced a structural remedy deficit that bankruptcy distributions have only partially and unevenly mitigated. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the article offers one of the first criminological analyses of the 2022 cryptocurrency collapses, grounded in state-corporate crime theory; specifies the boundary between regulatory lag and state facilitation; and conceptualises governance architecture as criminogenic infrastructure.

title: IoT Readiness in an Auto-Component SME: Barrier-Cost-KPI Prioritization using an Indian SME Readiness Index
summary: Indian Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) face significant structural challenges in adopting the Internet of Things (IoT), despite its transformative potential for enhancing manufacturing quality and operational efficiency. Existing readiness models often overlook the integrated impact of barrier severity, firm-specific cost structures, and quality-centric Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) unique to emerging economies. This research develops the Indian SME Readiness Index (ISRI) to provide a comprehensive prioritization framework for IoT adoption. Employing a quantitative single-case study methodology, the ISRI was applied to an auto-component SME in Aurangabad serving global OEMs. The framework utilizes barrier scoring across 15 validated indicators, cost factorization across 20 balance-sheet categories, and strategic KPI mapping. Key findings: “future viability and profitability”, “lack of IoT standards/architecture”, and “knowledge management deficits” as the most critical barriers threatening Parts Per Million (PPM) rates and delivery reliability. These results imply that IoT interventions must be prioritized based on their direct impact on quality-related financial risks. The study’s primary contribution is the ISRI framework, which fills a critical gap in context-specific readiness assessments for Indian SMEs. Practically, it offers an Excel-based diagnostic toolkit for managers to align digital transformation with quality objectives. While limited by its single-case focus, the research provides a robust foundation for future multi-sector validation, enabling evidence-based policymaking for cluster-level industrial growth.

title: Big Tech and Financial Services Convergence in Platform Based Financial Ecosystems
summary: The accelerating integration of digital technologies into financial ecosystems has reshaped competitive dynamics, as Big Tech firms increasingly expand beyond their core markets and encroach on traditional banking domains, creating a strategic inflection point for global financial services. This study aims to analyze how the convergence of Big Tech and financial services transforms value creation, market structure, and regulatory expectations, while identifying the strategic implications for incumbent institutions. Employing a qualitative research design that synthesizes systematic literature review, comparative industry analysis, and case based evaluation of leading global Big Tech firms, the study examines technological capabilities, platform business models, and cross sector expansion strategies to uncover emerging patterns within this evolving landscape. The findings indicate that the rise of embedded finance, data driven personalization, and AI enabled risk assessment empowers Big Tech to deliver highly efficient, scalable, and user-centric financial solutions that challenge banks’ traditional advantages in trust, compliance, and capital resources. Furthermore, the results reveal that incumbents adopting collaborative platform strategies, open banking initiatives, and digital transformation frameworks exhibit stronger competitive resilience than those relying solely on conventional product based models. The study concludes that the convergence of Big Tech and financial services necessitates a strategic reorientation for banks one that emphasizes innovation partnerships, data governance enhancement, and proactive regulatory engagement to sustain relevance and competitiveness within an increasingly platform dominated financial ecosystem.

title: From Digital Provision to Quality Improvement: A Resource-to-Capability Framework for Institutional Digital Ecosystems in Vocational Education and Training
summary: Abstract Purpose — This conceptual article considers how vocational education and training (VET) institutions may convert digital provision into capabilities that support pedagogical quality, rather than treating equipment or technology adoption as evidence of quality improvement. Design/methodology/approach — An interpretive synthesis connects research on digital transformation, organizational capabilities, VET teaching and process-based evaluation. It distinguishes resource availability, orchestration, capability enactment and quality evidence. Findings — A four-stage framework specifies digital provision, institutional resource orchestration, quality-enabling capabilities and pedagogical process quality, with external occupational interfaces and feedback cycles as boundary conditions. The propositions are theoretical and have not been empirically estimated. Originality — The contribution concerns the quality-oriented conversion of resources within VET institutions, not a generic claim that digitalization creates organizational capabilities. title: THE STRATEGIC IMPORTANCE OF USING BIG DATA, IOT, AND BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGIES IN DEVELOPING THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
summary: In the context of digital transformation, Big Data, IoT and Blockchain technologies are emerging as new drivers of economic development. The study aims to determine how these three technologies affect economic efficiency and management quality, and what synergy their integration creates. It uses content analysis of the scientific literature, a systems approach, comparative analysis and synthesis. The results show that Big Data improves analytical decision-making and expands the forecasting of economic processes; IoT ensures continuous production and lower costs through real-time monitoring; and Blockchain reduces transaction costs and strengthens institutional stability through transparency and trust. Integrated, the three technologies form a digital ecosystem with a synergistic effect on the drivers of economic growth. The discussion addresses barriers to adoption and the relevance of these technologies for Uzbekistan.

summary: The relevance of this study is determined by the rapid transformation of the digital advertising market, the intensifying fragmentation of the media landscape, and the growing complexity of enterprise marketing communications systems under conditions of digital transformation. Digital channels, with targeted advertising delivered through social media platforms, programmatic systems, and search networks at their core, have become a dominant component of enterprise communication budgets, reflecting a global shift toward automated, data-driven advertising ecosystems. However, despite its growing practical application, targeted advertising continues to be studied predominantly in isolation, detached from the broader system of integrated marketing communications (IMC) of the enterprise, which creates a substantial theoretical gap between digital marketing practice and the conceptual foundations of communications management. The present article addresses this gap by developing a conceptual model of targeted advertising integration into the enterprise marketing communications system. The study defines the dual structural position of targeted advertising within the communications mix under conditions of digital transformation - as both an independent communication tool and a technological method of addressable message delivery - distinguishing it from traditional mass advertising and clarifying its functional role alongside other tools such as content marketing, SMM, email marketing, and direct marketing. Three key properties of targeted advertising that enable its integrative role are identified: measurability, personalization, and interoperability. Based on a systematic analysis of scholarly literature and industry practice, four key mechanisms of synergistic interaction between targeted advertising and other communications instruments are identified and systematized: audience retargeting based on organic engagement data, cross-channel message reinforcement, sequential communication along the customer journey, and reverse data flow from advertising platforms to CRM systems and other channels. Based on this analysis, an author's conceptual model is proposed that visualizes the network architecture of bidirectional audience data flows between traditional and digital communication tools, with targeted advertising positioned as the central integrating node, and defines its functional role at each stage of the customer journey. To enable quantitative assessment of the identified synergistic effect, the article proposes an original indicator - the Integration Synergy Effect Coefficient - along with a methodological scheme for its verification based on a comparative research design. The proposed conceptual model and measurement toolkit provide a theoretically grounded and methodologically substantiated basis for transitioning enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized businesses, from isolated to integrated management of targeted advertising within their overall marketing communications strategy.

title: IoT-Enabled Predictive Analytics for Real-Time Decision-Making in Saudi Digital Service Platforms
summary: Saudi digital service platforms are now becoming more reliant on connected devices, the streaming of telemetry data, and automated service orchestration, but the shift from simply observing events to being able to anticipate operational outcomes is still very uneven. This review looks at how Internet of Things (IoT)-based predictive analytics can assist with real-time decision-making in the various digital service environments in Saudi Arabia, focusing on the architectural, analytical and governance conditions needed for a reliable implementation. The study draws together evidence from peer-reviewed publications between 2020 and 2025 covering the topics of IoT, edge intelligence, machine learning, digital platforms, decision support, privacy, reliability and smart-city applications. Instead of viewing prediction as a separate algorithmic activity, the review presents it as a complete operational capability that involves sensing, data-quality control, contextual processing, model inference, decision policies, workflow execution and feedback on the outcomes. The evidence shows that the value obtained depends more on a low-latency architecture, trustworthy data, explainable decision thresholds, resilient connectivity and institutional ownership of the results than on the complexity of the models. For Saudi Arabia, these requirements are especially important since the country's digital transformation includes large-scale investments in infrastructure, high levels of mobile connectivity, smart-city projects and sector-specific service platforms. A reference architecture and a decision lifecycle are suggested in order to link IoT telemetry with predictive service operations while still ensuring security, privacy and human oversight. The review concludes that the most defensible approach is a federated, edge-cloud operating model in which predictive intelligence is incorporated into measurable service workflows and is governed by clear assurance controls.

title: Implementing international standards for artificial intelligence regulation into corporate governance systems: a comparative legal analysis
summary: This thesis provides a comparative legal analysis of the implementation of international standards for artificial intelligence (AI) regulation into corporate governance systems. It examines instrumental and subject-oriented approaches to the legal status of AI in corporate law and outlines the requirements imposed on corporations by the OECD Principles (2019), UNESCO Recommendations (2021), and the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). The differences between Anglo-Saxon (United States, Delaware) and continental (Germany) models are identified in terms of directors’ fiduciary duties, the Business Judgment Rule, and liability for algorithmic decisions. Based on the identified gaps in Uzbekistan’s legislation, including the legal status of AI, the concept of a “governing body,” and the absence of independent AI audit mechanisms, proposals are made to strengthen AI’s legal framework and introduce recommendatory provisions into the Corporate Governance Code based on the “comply or explain” principle.

title: ALCAM Revisited: A System Dynamics Framework for Aircraft Life Cycle Costing under Contemporary Acquisition Conditions
summary: The global defense environment has undergone significant transformation since the original development of the Aircraft Life Cycle Cost Analysis Model (ALCAM), marked by great power competition, rapid technological disruption, and supply chain vulnerabilities. This research extends and updates the ALCAM framework to address contemporary defense acquisition challenges by incorporating digital transformation, supply chain resilience, sustainability requirements, and emerging technology integration. The study analyzes three primary procurement strategies: indigenous R&D, technology transfer with co-production, and off-the-shelf acquisition. Utilizing a generic System Dynamics simulation framework, the methodology captures non-linear relationships, feedback loops, and time-dependent variables across the system lifecycle. The enhanced model integrates Machine Learning estimates with simulation models to improve predictive capability and employs an internal numerical risk matrix to quantify uncertainties. Results demonstrate that life cycle cost differentials between procurement strategies have widened substantially due to supply chain vulnerabilities, accelerated technology obsolescence, and sustainment cost escalation. Simulation outcomes reveal that the off-the-shelf option, despite lower initial acquisition costs, projects significantly higher total life cycle costs due to long-term sustainment factors and foreign dependency premiums. The enhanced ALCAM framework provides defense decision-makers with a strategic planning tool that evaluates total ownership cost beyond traditional budgetary considerations, emphasizing the long-term value of indigenous development capabilities and technology sovereignty.

title: An Analysis of Tesla's Supply Chain Management Model
summary: As the global new energy vehicle (NEV) industry enters a phase of stock competition and high-quality development, supply chain management capabilities, cost optimization levels, and resilience to supply chain risks have become key sources of competitive differentiation among automakers, fundamentally changing the traditional automotive industry's emphasis on scale-based competition. Tesla, as a benchmark enterprise in the global NEV industry, has established a new supply chain management system that is underpinned by digitalization, features vertical integration as its core barrier, and integrates global layout with localized adaptation and coordination. The model also incorporates multiple supply sources and production locations to diversify supply chain risks. This paper takes Tesla's supply chain management model as the research object, systematically analyzing its core supply chain characteristics from three major frameworks: upstream supplier layout, midstream independent manufacturing of core technologies, and downstream direct-to-consumer (D2C) services. Additionally, it examines the practical challenges faced by Tesla's supply chain in the context of current global geopolitical conflicts, overseas policy barriers, and fluctuations in mineral resources. The study finds that the core advantages of Tesla's supply chain model lie in eliminating information silos across the entire chain through digital technology, gaining control over costs and technology through independent research and production in core areas, and achieving cost reduction, efficiency improvement, and risk diversification through a globally dispersed layout and deep localization adaptation. However, the model also has limitations, including limited resilience to supply disruptions resulting from a streamlined supplier base and substantial exposure to foreign-market policy changes.
